patterns.title: Text Filtering and Pattern Matching (grep)
patterns.short_description: Filters file lines matching regular expression patterns or fixed strings using grep, egrep, or grep -E.
mental_triggers: Search for valid phone numbers in a text file
Filter log entries matching error codes
Invert match to exclude comments and empty lines with grep -v
constraint_signals: Line-based stream filtering with standard POSIX or extended regular expressions
patterns.complexity: Time: O(N * L) where N is line count, L is average line length | Space: O(L) stream buffer

dialect_notes.bash: LeetCode runs bash on Linux; GNU and BSD versions of sed, grep and sort differ (for example sed -i, grep -P).

patterns.base_template_sh:
# Read and filter lines matching a regex pattern
grep -P "^(\([0-9]{3}\) |[0-9]{3}-)[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}$" file.txt

patterns.title: Delimited Field Extraction and Transformation (awk / cut)
patterns.short_description: Parses delimited text files into columns, reformatting and extracting specific fields using awk or cut.
mental_triggers: Extract column 2 from space-separated or comma-separated log
Transpose or reorder fields in a structured report
Filter rows where column value satisfies numeric comparison (e.g. awk '$2 > 50')
constraint_signals: Structured columnar input where delimiter can be whitespace, tab, or custom character
patterns.complexity: Time: O(N * L) single-pass stream processing | Space: O(L) per-line buffer

dialect_notes.bash: LeetCode runs bash on Linux; GNU and BSD versions of sed, grep and sort differ (for example sed -i, grep -P).

patterns.title: Stream Editing and In-Place Substitution (sed)
patterns.short_description: Transforms text streams by performing regex substitutions, line insertions, deletions, or specific line extractions (sed).
mental_triggers: Print exactly the 10th line of a file (sed -n '10p')
Replace target keyword across text stream without loading whole file into memory
Delete trailing whitespace or leading comment blocks
constraint_signals: One-pass stream transformation with low memory overhead
patterns.complexity: Time: O(N * L) stream scan | Space: O(L) pattern buffer

dialect_notes.bash: LeetCode runs bash on Linux; GNU and BSD versions of sed, grep and sort differ (for example sed -i, grep -P).

patterns.base_template_sh:
# Extract Nth line directly without reading entire file
sed -n "10p" file.txt

patterns.title: Frequency Counting and Sorting (sort / uniq)
patterns.short_description: Counts item frequencies, removes adjacent duplicates, and orders output lines using the standard sort | uniq -c pipeline.
mental_triggers: Calculate word frequencies in a text file
Find top 10 most frequent IP addresses in web server access log
Sort words by descending frequency followed by alphabetical tie-breaker
constraint_signals: uniq requires sorted input to detect duplicate occurrences; sort -n for numeric, -r for reverse
patterns.complexity: Time: O(N log N) sorting + O(N) frequency aggregation | Space: O(N) temporary buffer

dialect_notes.bash: LeetCode runs bash on Linux; GNU and BSD versions of sed, grep and sort differ (for example sed -i, grep -P).

patterns.base_template_sh:
# Tokenize words, compute frequencies, and sort descending
cat words.txt | tr -s " " "
" | sort | uniq -c | sort -r | awk "{print \, \}"

patterns.title: Line-by-Line File Processing and State Tracking
patterns.short_description: Iterates through text streams line by line using bash while read loops or head/tail windowing, tracking state across lines.
mental_triggers: Read a file line-by-line preserving leading/trailing whitespace (IFS= read -r line)
Inspect fixed line windows (e.g. tail -n +10 | head -n 1)
Maintain stateful accumulators or multi-line state machines in bash
constraint_signals: Subshell variable scoping in pipelines; read loops must avoid pipeline subshell gotchas or use process substitution
patterns.complexity: Time: O(N * L) line-by-line evaluation | Space: O(L) single line variable

dialect_notes.bash: LeetCode runs bash on Linux; GNU and BSD versions of sed, grep and sort differ (for example sed -i, grep -P).

patterns.base_template_sh:
# Process file line-by-line preserving whitespace
while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "" ]; do
    echo ""
done < file.txt

hints.title: Position-Targeted Line Extraction
hints.text: A specific line number must be retrieved from a text file, producing no output if the file contains fewer lines. How can a text utility extract exactly one target line index without redundant scanning?

hints.title: Stream Editing Address Printing
hints.text: Stream editors allow addressing individual line numbers directly, suppressing default output and selectively printing only the addressed line.

hints.title: Sed Targeted Print Command
hints.text: Run sed with the -n flag to suppress default printing, and supply the script 10p pointing to file.txt. If the file has 10 or more lines, line 10 is printed. If it contains fewer, no output is emitted.

variables: N: number of lines in file.txt
complexity.notes: Streaming single-pass line inspection with early exit capability.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Slurping the entire file into memory with cat file.txt | head -n 10 | tail -n 1 spawns multiple pipeline processes and consumes buffer memory proportional to file size, failing or slowing down when files have fewer than 10 lines.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: sed -n '10p' file.txt streams line-by-line using O(1) constant buffer space and prints only line 10, executing in O(N) streaming time (or early-exiting with 10q on large files).
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Handling files with fewer than 10 lines cleanly (must output nothing); avoiding multiple spawned subshells when a single stream editor tool suffices.

solutions.approach: Sed Stream Addressing with Suppressed Default Print

hints.title: Column-to-Row Inversion
hints.text: Transposing tabular data requires gathering words in the same horizontal column across all lines and outputting them as a single line. How can an associative array buffer words indexed by column?

hints.title: Associative Field Accumulation
hints.text: Iterate through each row record. For field index i from 1 to the number of fields, append the field value to an accumulator array keyed by i, prepending a space if an entry already exists.

hints.title: Buffer Flushing in Final Block
hints.text: Use an awk program with a row loop that builds array entries for each column index. In the completion action block, iterate from 1 to the field count and print each combined column string.

hints.title: Complete Implementation

variables: R: number of rows in file.txt
C: number of columns in file.txt
complexity.notes: Single stream traversal buffering matrix tokens into associative arrays before flushing transposed lines.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Reading the entire file with repeated head and cut invocations in nested loops incurs O(R * C^2) process spawn overhead and fails on larger files.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Buffering transposed tokens in awk memory provides linear single-pass performance at the cost of proportional string memory.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Handling variable numbers of rows and columns cleanly and managing spaces between concatenated tokens without trailing whitespace.

solutions.approach: Field Processing via Associative Array Accumulation in awk

hints.title: Pattern Validation Across Records
hints.text: Phone numbers must conform strictly to two distinct standard notations without extraneous leading or trailing characters. How can lines matching either specification be isolated from invalid text?

hints.title: Anchored Regular Expression Filter
hints.text: Line filtering tools support regular expression patterns. Anchoring expressions to both start and end boundaries ensures partial matches on malformed lines are rejected.

hints.title: Regex Disjunction with Grep
hints.text: Use grep -E with line anchors ^ and $ to match either format: three digits enclosed in parentheses followed by a space and standard four-digit suffix, or three digits separated by hyphens. Print matching lines directly from file.txt.

variables: N: number of lines in file.txt
complexity.notes: DFA regex matching per line buffer without loading full file into memory.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Reading line by line with a shell while read loop executes interpreted subshell commands per line, running hundreds of times slower than native compiled regex matchers. Loose regexes match substrings inside longer invalid numbers.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: grep -E utilizes a compiled deterministic finite automaton (DFA) in O(N) streaming time with O(1) memory per line buffer.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Anchoring with ^ and $ to prevent partial matches; handling both formats (xxx) xxx-xxxx and xxx-xxx-xxxx in a single combined extended regex.

hints.title: Stream Tokenization and Ranking
hints.text: Input text contains varying whitespace separating terms across lines. How can an arbitrary text stream be split into individual words, counted, and ordered by occurrence in descending order?

hints.title: Pipelined Word Aggregation
hints.text: Standard command-line utilities can transform whitespace into line breaks, aggregate duplicate adjacent tokens to count frequencies, and sort numerically.

hints.title: Pipelined Unix Text Processing
hints.text: Read words.txt and translate runs of whitespace into newlines using tr -s. Filter blank lines, sort the tokens alphabetically, count unique occurrences with uniq -c, sort numerically in descending order using sort -nr, and reformat columns to display the word followed by its count.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```bash
cat words.txt | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | grep -v '^$' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | awk '{print $2 " " $1}'
```

variables: W: total word count in words.txt
complexity.notes: Unix pipeline tokenizing, sorting, counting, and ranking word frequencies.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Writing a nested shell loop with multiple file rereads takes quadratic time. Without collapsing multiple consecutive spaces and empty lines, downstream token counts are corrupted.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: A Unix pipeline (tr -s -> sort -> uniq -c -> sort -nr) processes data via streaming IPC buffers in O(W log W) time with O(W) external sort buffer space.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Tokenizing whitespace properly with tr -s '[:space:]' '\n'; sorting descending by frequency; outputting <word> <frequency> format.

solutions.code: cat words.txt | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | grep -v '^$' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | awk '{print $2 " " $1}'
solutions.approach: Pipelined tr, sort, uniq -c and awk
